title: Sa Re Ga - Your First Three Notes
description: Open your first finger holes, hear the intervals, and play a short phrase with three notes.

tasks.title: Meet Re and Ga
content: Re (Rishabh) is the second note - lift your bottom finger to play it. Ga (Gandhar) is the third - lift two bottom fingers.

items: Sa (all holes closed) - the home note
Re (lift bottom finger) - a calm, gentle step up
Ga (lift two bottom fingers) - bright and cheerful

content.text: Lift fingers cleanly and completely. A half-lifted finger makes a fuzzy, unclear note.

content: These three notes - Sa, Re, Ga - are the foundation of countless melodies in Indian music. Master them and everything else builds on top.

questions.prompt: Which finger do you lift first to go from Sa to Re?

options.text: The top finger (closest to the blowing hole)
options.why: Notes go from bottom to top on a bansuri.

options.text: The bottom finger (farthest from the blowing hole)

options.why: That would give you Ga, not Re.

questions.prompt: I understand the fingering for Sa, Re, and Ga

hints: On the bansuri, notes ascend by lifting fingers from the bottom of the flute upward.

tasks.title: Fingering quiz
content: Before you pick up the flute, let's make sure you know exactly which holes to open for each note.
On a six-hole bansuri, the holes are numbered 1 (closest to the blowing hole) through 6 (farthest).

questions.prompt: To play Sa, how many finger holes should be closed?

options.yes: Correct! Sa is all holes closed - the lowest note in the middle octave.

options.why: Opening one hole gives you Re, not Sa.
All holes open gives you a much higher note.

questions.prompt: To play Re, which hole do you open?

options.why: Opening hole 1 would give you a higher note, not Re.

options.yes: Right! Open the bottom hole for Re.

options.why: Opening two bottom holes gives you Ga.

questions.prompt: How many finger holes do you open to play Ga? Type the number.
questions.yes: Correct! Open holes 5 and 6 (the two bottom holes) for Ga.
questions.no: Open the two bottom holes (5 and 6) for Ga.

hints: The pattern is simple: Sa = 0 holes open, Re = 1 hole open, Ga = 2 holes open.
Always count from the bottom of the flute.

tasks.title: Hear the difference
content: Listen to each note and identify it. You will hear Sa, Re, or Ga played one at a time.
Close your eyes if it helps you concentrate. Focus on how each note feels - Sa is grounded, Re is a gentle step up, Ga is bright and open.
hints: Sa is the lowest of the three - it sounds grounded and stable.
Re is one step above Sa - slightly brighter.
Ga is the highest of the three - it has an open, cheerful quality.

tasks.title: Hold Re steady
content: Now pick up your flute. Lift only the bottom finger and blow a steady stream of air to play Re.
Your goal: hold Re for 3 seconds without the pitch wobbling. Keep the other five fingers firmly closed.
hints: Make sure your bottom finger lifts completely clear of the hole.
Keep the other five fingers pressed flat - any leak will shift the pitch.
Blow gently and steadily. Too much air makes the note jump to the upper octave.

tasks.title: Hold Ga steady
content: Now lift two bottom fingers to play Ga. The more holes you open, the more precisely you need to seal the remaining ones.
Hold Ga for 3 seconds with a clear, steady tone.
hints: With two holes open, air leaks from the remaining fingers matter more. Press firmly.
If the note sounds airy or weak, adjust your lip position slightly.
Ga should sound bright and clear - not breathy.

tasks.title: Play Sa Re Ga
content: Now play the ascending phrase: Sa, Re, Ga. Take your time between notes and make each one clear.
The key is clean transitions. Lift each finger decisively - don't let it hover halfway.

questions.prompt: Play Sa Re Ga in order.

hints: Lift each finger cleanly - don't slide between positions.
Keep your breath steady as you change fingers.
If a note sounds unclear, pause, reset, and try that note alone first.

tasks.title: Come back down
content: Going down is just as important. Play Ga, Re, Sa - descending back to your home note.
Descending requires you to place fingers back down. Each finger must land squarely on its hole to seal it.
hints: Place each finger back firmly - a loose finger leaks air and muddies the note.
Descending is often harder than ascending. Take it slower if needed.
Think of your fingers 'finding home' on each hole.

tasks.title: Ascending and descending
content: Now combine both directions in one phrase: Sa Re Ga Re Sa.
This is called an alankar - a melodic exercise pattern. Alankars build fluency the same way scales do in Western music.

content.text: Take your time at the top (Ga) before descending. Rushing the turn is the most common beginner mistake.

questions.prompt: Play Sa Re Ga Re Sa.
What is the name for a melodic exercise pattern in Indian music?
questions.yes: Correct! Alankars are the backbone of Indian music practice.
questions.no: It's called an alankar - a melodic exercise pattern.

hints: Break it into two halves if it helps: Sa Re Ga (pause) Re Sa.
Keep your breath continuous through the whole phrase.
An alankar is a practice pattern - like playing scales but with musical shapes.

tasks.title: Your first melody
content: Now let's make music. Play this simple melody: Sa Re Ga Ga Re Sa.

Notice how repeating Ga at the top gives the phrase a shape - it lingers at the peak before returning home. This is how melodies work: not just going up and down, but pausing and emphasising certain notes.

questions.prompt: Play Sa Re Ga Ga Re Sa.
Why does repeating Ga make the melody more musical?

options.why: Length alone does not make something musical.

options.text: It creates emphasis and shape - the melody dwells on the high point
options.yes: Exactly! Lingering on a note gives the phrase direction and emotion.

options.text: It is a rule you must always follow
options.why: There are no such rules - it is a musical choice.

options.text: It is easier to play than other patterns
options.why: Difficulty is not the reason - it is about musical expression.

hints: Think of the two Ga notes as the top of an arch.
Let the second Ga ring a moment longer before descending.
If you lose the phrase, hum it to yourself first.

tasks.title: Final challenge
content: One last test. Play this five-note phrase from memory: Ga Re Sa Re Ga.
This phrase starts and ends on Ga, with Sa as the low point in the middle. It is a common shape in Indian melodies - descending to the home note and rising back up.

content.text: If you can play this cleanly, you have solid command of your first three notes. Well done!

questions.prompt: Play Ga Re Sa Re Ga.
Final ear check: identify these notes.

hints: Start with all fingers up for Ga, then walk them down and back up.
The pattern is a V-shape: start high, go low, come back high.
Take a breath before you begin - this is the longest phrase yet.
